article.overview: An electrostatic dust analyser is an instrument designed to measure fine dust particles that are lofted from the lunar surface by electrostatic forces. For each particle it aims to determine the charge, velocity, size (through mass) and flux. The best-documented example is the Electrostatic Dust Analyzer (EDA), described by Wang et al. (2024) as a high-fidelity, flight-qualified prototype that reached Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6 under NASA's Development and Advancement of Lunar Instrumentation (DALI) programme. The reviewed sources do not show that any EDA has yet flown to the Moon.
article.description: The instrument measures dust particles as they pass through an electric-field-based sensing arrangement. The EDA paper describes two identical dust trajectory sensor (DTS) units, one at each end of the instrument, with a deflection field electrode (DFE) unit between them. The instrument also has two electron rejection grid units. There are two wire-electrode arrays in each DTS, seven wires per array, giving four arrays and 28 wires in total. Each wire feeds its own charge-sensitive amplifier with a stated bandwidth of 3.2 Hz to 1 kHz. As a charged particle passes through, the charge it induces on the wire arrays gives its total charge and its path, from which its velocity is derived. Its size is inferred from how strongly the DFE deflects it. The instrument is intended to characterise dust that is electrostatically lofted above the lunar surface, a process that has been studied for more than fifty years but has lacked direct in situ measurement. The EDA is a lineage successor of the Electrostatic Lunar Dust Analyzer (ELDA), first described by Duncan et al. (2011) as a wire-electrode detector for slow-moving dust particles.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The primary purpose of an electrostatic dust analyser is to measure the properties of dust that is charged and lofted by the lunar environment. According to Wang et al. (2024), the measurements are intended to assess dust hazards to crews and to exploration systems, and to inform how the surfaces of the Moon and other airless bodies evolve. Measured quantities are dust charge, velocity, size (mass) and flux. Dust charging and transport are relevant to several open questions. Apollo-era crews reported a faint horizon glow near the Moon, which was interpreted as scattering from a high-altitude dust layer. LADEE measurements did not find dust densities high enough to produce such a glow, and the origin of the glow is still described as unresolved (Universe Today, 2014). An in situ dust analyser can provide the direct particle-level measurements needed to test these ideas. A separate 2025 conference abstract by Nardi et al. notes that in situ measurements of charged lunar dust near the surface are still lacking.
article.operating_principle: The EDA operates by sensing the electrical signature of individual dust grains as they cross a sensing volume. Each dust trajectory sensor has a set of wire electrodes. When a charged grain passes close to a wire, it induces a charge signal on that wire, and the charge-sensitive amplifier records the signal shape and amplitude. Combining signals from the wires in both trajectory sensors gives the particle's total charge and its trajectory, from which its velocity vector is reconstructed. The deflection field electrode applies an electric field across the path of the grain. A heavier (larger) grain is deflected less than a lighter one at the same velocity, so the change in trajectory provides a size or mass estimate. Electron rejection grids, biased between 0 V and -125 V in the reported design, limit the effect of electrons on the measurement. The earlier ELDA concept used the same general approach of an array of wire electrodes and an electrostatic deflection region, with mass inferred from the change in velocity before and after deflection (Sternovsky et al., 2013).
article.scientific_importance: Dust on airless bodies is a hazard for optics, thermal surfaces, seals and crew, as well as a possible scientific record of the surface environment. Electrostatic lofting is one proposed mechanism by which fine grains are moved above the surface. Direct, particle-level measurements of charge, velocity, size and flux would test these mechanisms, which current remote observations can only infer indirectly. Such measurements would also provide ground truth for the dust-environment models that engineers use when planning surface operations.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal mass, size or power value for an electrostatic dust analyser. The values below describe the specific EDA prototype reported by Wang et al. (2024) and the earlier ELDA laboratory prototype. Values are not generalised to other designs, and the EDA's stated mass and power refer to its sensor module, not to a complete flight instrument with its digital signal processing (DSP) module.

examples.name: Electrostatic Lunar Dust Analyzer (ELDA) prototype
examples.sensor_configuration: Array of wire electrodes with an electrostatic deflection region. Velocity vector reconstructed from signal shapes and amplitudes.
examples.performance_as_reported: A 2013 laboratory paper reports that a full prototype was tested under vacuum and that particle mass could be measured to within a factor of two even at very low signal-to-noise ratio (Sternovsky et al., 2013, as summarised in secondary sources). Exact specifications were not verified against the full text.
examples.qualification: Laboratory prototype only; no flight or flight-qualification claim is made for ELDA in the reviewed sources.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The EDA's external dimensions are not stated in the reviewed sources, so they are recorded as not publicly specified. The instrument's geometry is set by its two dust trajectory sensors, its central deflection field electrode and its 8 cm wire-electrode length. These features determine the sensing volume, which in turn affects the measurable size, velocity and flux ranges. The ELDA prototype's dimensions are likewise not stated in the reviewed sources.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The EDA sensor module is reported at 4.3 kg in Wang et al. (2024). This figure does not include the DSP module, which the paper states was outside the scope of the prototype development. A 2023 DAP conference slide deck was reported in a secondary search summary to list a mass of 5.5 kg and power of 7.5 W. That deck could not be read in full, so these values are not used as specifications here and the difference from the paper's figures is recorded as an open item in data_quality_notes.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The EDA sensor module is reported at 5 W in Wang et al. (2024). The paper's definition of this power value should be checked against the full text before it is used for mission power budgets. The deflection field electrode operates at plus or minus 125 V for lunar-surface use, according to the paper; the 1500 V figure is the laboratory test condition, not a flight operating value.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar dust analyser must operate in vacuum, across large surface temperature swings, and in a setting where dust itself is a contamination hazard for sensors and electronics. The EDA prototype was tested against GSFC-STD-7000 (GEVS) levels, with vibration at 14.1 grms, quasi-static loads of 42 g, a survival thermal cycle from -50 to +85 degrees Celsius and operational thermal cycles from -35 to +80 degrees Celsius, as reported in Wang et al. (2024). The sensing electrodes are exposed by design to charged dust, so the instrument must avoid electrical interference from its own surroundings. The reviewed paper reports electron rejection grids and a surface deflection voltage of plus or minus 125 V, but not a full electromagnetic compatibility assessment. The EDA's suitability for a given lunar surface location, thermal environment or rover configuration has not been established in the reviewed sources.
article.limitations: The EDA's flight status is the main limitation. Wang et al. (2024) describe a flight-qualified prototype at TRL 6, and the 2025 DUSTER funding announcement describes future instruments that will be built at LASP; neither source reports a launch or an operating instrument. Its measurable ranges are bounded: dust radius from about 1 to 20 micrometres, velocity from about 0.8 to 20 metres per second, charge from about 1.2 to 64 femtocoulombs and flux up to about 1.7 particles per square centimetre per second, according to the paper's stated performance. These ranges are not the same as the requirement ranges. A single instrument also cannot establish the spatial distribution of dust across the Moon, so measurements would need to be combined with other sites or orbital observations.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The EDA is an instrument rather than a complete lander payload. Public information on its planned delivery is limited to the DUSTER project, which was selected under NASA's Artemis Deployed Instruments Program. According to the LASP announcement (2025), both DUSTER instruments, including the EDA, are to be housed on the Mobile Autonomous Prospecting Platform (MAPP) rover supplied by Lunar Outpost. Dust measurements in that configuration would be taken by a rover-mounted instrument rather than a fixed surface station.
transportation_process: Integrate the EDA sensor module and associated electronics into the rover or host platform on Earth (planned, as reported for DUSTER).
Launch the host spacecraft and rover using a launch vehicle that is not identified in the reviewed sources.
Transfer to the Moon and deliver the rover to the surface with a lander that is not identified in the reviewed sources.
Deploy the rover and operate the EDA on its platform.
Connect the instrument to the rover's power and data interfaces. The interface details are not stated in the reviewed sources.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The EDA is planned to be carried on a rover (MAPP) rather than deployed on its own. No separate deployment mechanism for the EDA is described in the reviewed sources. The exact placement, orientation and thermal control on the rover are not stated.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No EDA has been reported as deployed on the Moon in the sources reviewed. The NASA Electrodynamic Dust Shield (EDS), which is a different instrument, flew on Firefly's Blue Ghost lander in 2025 (Young, 2025). It should not be confused with the EDA.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any named lander or rover is not verified. The MAPP rover is identified as the planned host for DUSTER, but the reviewed sources give no mass, power, interface or delivery schedule that would confirm compatibility with a specific Artemis or CLPS delivery. The sensor module mass and power values in Wang et al. (2024) would need to be compared with verified host-platform allocations before any compatibility statement could be made.

article.historical_significance: The ELDA concept was first described by Duncan et al. (2011) as an instrument for detecting and tracking slow-moving dust particles that are lifted from the lunar surface. A full laboratory prototype was tested under vacuum by 2013 (Sternovsky et al., 2013). The EDA developed from that work and reached TRL 6 under the DALI programme. The DUSTER project, which carries the EDA, was selected under NASA's Artemis Deployed Instruments Program with $24.8 million in funding to build its instruments (LASP, 2025). The significance of the EDA therefore lies in its development path toward a first direct in situ measurement of electrostatically lofted lunar dust, rather than in any completed mission result.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The most important uncertainties are: (1) whether any EDA has flown, which the reviewed sources do not show; (2) the EDA's mass, power and dimensions, where the paper gives sensor-module figures and a slide-based secondary summary gives different values that could not be checked; (3) the source of the Table 1 performance values, which should be confirmed in the full paper; (4) the planned mission, launch date and host-platform interfaces for DUSTER, none of which are stated in the reviewed sources; (5) the ELDA prototype's specifications, which are known only from secondary summaries; and (6) the CubeSat variant CEDA, which is mentioned in a conference paper that was not read in full and is therefore not described in this article beyond a note. The horizon-glow explanation remains unresolved in the reviewed sources.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL fields in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs are included because no direct image asset for the EDA could be verified from an official source.

data_quality_notes: Flight status: Wang et al. (2024) describe the EDA as a flight-qualified prototype at TRL 6. The reviewed sources do not show any EDA having flown. The 2025 DUSTER announcement describes future instruments. The article treats the EDA as not flown.

Mass and power discrepancy: the paper gives a sensor-module mass of 4.3 kg and power of 5 W. A DAP 2023 slide deck, known only from a secondary search summary, gives 5.5 kg and 7.5 W. The deck could not be read (the fetched PDF returned binary content and no text). Both sets of values are recorded here, and the paper's values are used as the primary source. The discrepancy is unresolved and may reflect different system boundaries (for example, including the DSP module).

Measurement performance values (Table 1 of Wang et al., 2024) are taken from the paper's abstract-level page on the DOI landing page. The full text was not read in full, so the measurement context (laboratory or modelled) should be confirmed.

ELDA specifications, the 2011 Duncan et al. paper and the 2013 Sternovsky et al. paper were not read in full. Their bibliographic details come from secondary aggregator and search records. No verifiable URL was obtained, so they are cited in prose only and are not in the numbered references list.
CEDA (CubeSat variant with a 2U dust analyser module) was mentioned in secondary search results but the conference paper was not read; it is not described as an example.

No verified direct image asset for the EDA was found. The search surfaced a schematic in a 2019 EPSC-DPS abstract (EPSC-DPS2019-276) and a CEDA photograph, but neither was retrieved or verified as an EDA image, so no image entries were added.
The Apollo 17 horizon glow and LADEE finding are cited from secondary news coverage; primary Apollo and LADEE papers were not read.
The Electrodynamic Dust Shield (EDS), flown on Blue Ghost in 2025, is a different instrument and is not part of this payload.

Search queries and page reads: 7 web searches and 11 page-read attempts. Several page reads failed (HTTP 403 on DOAJ and core.ac.uk; connection refused on a libmast mirror; binary PDF content on two conference PDFs; redirects not followed on an APPEL page). The PSJ paper was read via its IOP Publishing landing page.
